summary: This unit teaches you to promote diversity and inclusion in a Jamaican public body or business. You will learn what diversity, inclusion, bias and discrimination mean, how the law and policy protect people, how to make recruitment, employment and services fair and accessible, how to lead an inclusive team, deal with unfair treatment, and how to measure progress with simple data.

blocks.p: **Diversity** is the range of differences among the people in a workforce and among the public it serves. **Inclusion** is making sure that every one of those people feels valued, respected and able to take part fully. A manager promotes diversity by making sure that people are treated fairly, that barriers are removed, that different views are heard, and that services reach everyone.

This unit is for supervisors and managers at Level 5 in ministries, agencies, municipal corporations, schools and businesses. Jamaica's motto, "Out of Many, One People", reflects a society with many backgrounds, but unfair treatment still exists. Women, persons with disabilities, young and older workers, people from rural parishes, people of different religions, people living with HIV and others can face barriers that managers must see and remove.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in your unit
rows: Explain diversity and inclusion
Define the terms, name visible and less visible differences, and explain why they matter to a public body.
Recognise bias and discrimination
Spot stereotypes, prejudice, unconscious bias, direct and indirect discrimination, and harassment.
Apply the legal and policy framework
Follow the Constitution's rights, the law on disability, the law on harassment, data protection and agency policy, and ask HR or the legal unit when unsure.
Make recruitment and employment fair
Advertise widely, use the same criteria for all, avoid unlawful questions and make reasonable accommodations.
Make services accessible
Remove physical, communication and language barriers, and consult users.
Lead an inclusive team
Run meetings that hear every voice, use positive action properly and deal with unfair treatment.
Develop policy and measure progress
Write, launch and monitor a diversity and inclusion policy, using confidential data and trends.

ul: A multiple-choice theory paper with scenario questions on bias, discrimination, accommodations, accessibility, policy and measurement.
A written paper with short answers (exact terms, simple percentages) and longer answers in which you plan a policy, an audit or a response to a complaint.
Group practicals: an inclusion and accessibility audit with an action plan, and a short diversity awareness session for public officers.

blocks.note: Learn the difference between direct and indirect discrimination and between diversity and inclusion. They are asked in many forms.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: Diversity
The mix of differences among people
A team with men and women, young and older officers, and staff from several parishes
Inclusion
How far each person feels valued and able to take part
A quiet officer's ideas are asked for and used in meetings
Equality
Treating people fairly and giving the same opportunities
Every applicant is scored against the same written criteria
Equity
Giving people what they need to reach a fair result
A screen-reading programme for an officer who is partially sighted

blocks.p: Diversity without inclusion fails. A unit can hire a mixed team and still lose them if the culture ignores or isolates some people. **Diversity is the mix; inclusion is how involved people feel.**

Some differences can be seen: age, sex, skin colour, some disabilities. Many cannot. A manager may not know about a person's religion, sexual orientation, long-term health condition (such as diabetes, epilepsy or HIV), caring duties, mental health, first language or education unless the person chooses to share it. Never assume. Create a climate in which people can share if they wish and never push them to.

blocks.h: Why diversity matters to a public body

ul: A workforce that reflects the people it serves **understands and serves the public better**.
Different views improve decisions and reduce "group think". A policy team made up entirely of people of the same age and background may miss the needs of other groups in the country.
Fair treatment keeps good staff, raises morale and reduces complaints, absence and grievances.
A public body must be seen to be fair; unfair treatment harms trust and may break the law.
Services designed for everyone work better for everyone.

blocks.h: Problems when diversity is poorly managed

ul: Conflict, misunderstanding and unfair jokes or remarks
Talented people leaving, or never applying
Complaints, grievances and possible legal claims
Poor decisions because only some views are heard
Damage to the body's reputation

blocks.h: Key terms of bias and unfairness

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: Stereotype
A fixed, over-simple belief about what all members of a group are like
"Older applicants struggle with computers."
Prejudice
An unfair opinion about a person or group, formed before knowing the facts
Doubting a young woman's ability to lead before she has done anything
Unconscious (implicit) bias
Attitudes and beliefs we hold without being aware of them
Favouring candidates who went to the same school as you
Discrimination
Treating a person unfairly because of a personal characteristic
Not shortlisting someone because of their religion
Direct discrimination
Treating a person openly less well because of a characteristic
Refusing to interview a qualified woman because she is pregnant
Indirect discrimination
A rule that applies to all but puts one group at an unfair disadvantage and is not needed for the job
Requiring all field officers to be 1.8 m tall when height is not needed
Harassment
Unwanted conduct that violates a person's dignity or creates a hostile or humiliating setting
Repeated jokes about someone's accent, or unwelcome sexual remarks
Victimisation
Treating someone badly because they raised a complaint or helped another to do so
Giving a worker the worst shifts after she reported unfair treatment
Tokenism
A small, surface effort to look inclusive
One appointment of a woman to a board, to avoid criticism, with no real role for her

blocks.note: A rule that looks neutral can still be indirect discrimination. The test is its effect on one group and whether the rule is really needed for the job.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Unconscious bias: how to reduce its effect

ul: Use **written criteria** and score each application or candidate against them.
Where possible, shortlist from applications with names and personal details removed.
Use a diverse panel; one person's bias then carries less weight.
Slow down before making decisions that affect people.
Check outcomes: who is being chosen, promoted or disciplined?
Use training that includes real cases, discussion and follow-up, not only a one-off lecture.

blocks.p: Public bodies must act within the law. In this kit, laws are named by their **purpose**; ask the human resource or legal unit for the exact provisions and current rules.

head: Source
What it does
rows: The Constitution (Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms)
Protects the rights and freedoms of everyone in Jamaica, including equality before the law and freedom of conscience and religion
The law on persons with disabilities
Protects the rights of persons with disabilities, including in employment, services and access
The law on sexual harassment
Protects workers and others from sexual harassment and requires employers to prevent it and act on it
Employment and labour law
Sets fair treatment, grievance and dismissal rules
The data protection law
Controls how personal information, including sensitive information about health or religion, is collected, used and stored
Public service rules and agency policy
Set standards for recruitment, conduct, grievances and handling of complaints

ul: Know the main rights and the agency's policies.
If a planned rule or decision may be unlawful, **seek advice from the human resource or legal unit** before acting.
Treat grievances and complaints seriously and follow the procedure.
Protect people who complain in good faith from retaliation.
Keep sensitive information, such as health or religion, confidential and use it only for its purpose.

blocks.p: If an officer tells you in confidence that he is living with HIV, **keep it confidential** and ask whether he needs any support. Do not tell colleagues or the manager above you unless the officer agrees or the law requires. People who fear that private matters will spread will not ask for help.

flow: Define the job and the real requirements (the person specification)
Advertise widely: online, in the press, in rural parishes and through community and disability organisations
Use plain language and accessible formats for the advertisement and application
Shortlist against the same written criteria, with more than one person scoring
Use a diverse interview panel and the same core questions for every candidate
Appoint on merit, keep records of reasons, and give honest feedback
Review the process: who applied, who was shortlisted and who was appointed

blocks.p: If the aim is to attract more applicants from certain groups, such as rural parishes, widen the reach of your advertising rather than lower your standards.

head: Fine to ask
Not fine to ask
rows: Can you do the essential duties of the job, with or without adjustment?
Are you planning to have children in the next few years?
Tell us about a time you resolved a customer complaint.
How old are you, and when do you plan to retire?
Are you available for the working hours the job requires?
Are you married? Who looks after your children?
What experience do you have in using spreadsheets?
What church do you attend, and what do your parents do?

blocks.p: Questions about marriage, pregnancy, religion, health, age and family cannot be linked to the job and invite discrimination. Ask all candidates the same questions, and score answers against the criteria.

A **reasonable accommodation** is a change to the work, work setting or the way things are done that allows a person with a disability to do the job or take part equally. It is "reasonable" when it does not impose an undue burden on the employer.

head: Situation
Accommodation
rows: New officer who is partially sighted
Screen-reading software, a larger monitor, good lighting
Officer who uses a wheelchair posted to an upstairs unit with no lift
Talk with the officer, then arrange a ground-floor workspace or move the unit
Officer with a hearing impairment
Written notes of meetings, a visual alert for the phone, a sign language interpreter for key meetings
Officer with a long-term illness
Flexible hours for medical appointments, a quiet workspace

blocks.p: Always **talk with the officer first**. People know what helps them. Do not assume, and do not make them feel a burden.

blocks.h: Work and family needs, religion and culture

ul: Consider flexible-start requests (for example a single father who needs to take his child to school) fairly, against the needs of the work, and apply the same fairness to others.

A request to avoid work on a religious day of rest, such as a Seventh-day Adventist officer who observes the Sabbath from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, should be considered fairly, and the roster adjusted if the work allows.
Plan staff events with attention to dietary, religious and health needs: ask staff beforehand.
Mix older and younger officers: pairs can share experience and new skills.

blocks.note: "Consider fairly" means looking for a workable arrangement. It does not mean automatic approval, and it does not mean automatic refusal.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Barrier
Example
Possible solution
rows: Physical
No ramp, narrow doors, high counters, no accessible toilet
Ramps, wide doorways, a lowered counter, ground-floor service points
Communication
A Deaf customer cannot be understood; signs are unclear
A Jamaican Sign Language (JSL) interpreter or written exchange; clear signs
Language and literacy
Long legal forms that patients struggle to complete
Plain language forms, help to complete them, large print
Information
Services announced only online
Use radio, notices, community meetings and phone as well
Attitude
Staff speak down to older or rural customers
Training, service standards and feedback

ul: Use short sentences and everyday words; explain unavoidable technical terms.
Use gender-neutral words: "chair" not "chairman", "staff" not "manpower", "applicants" or "they" instead of "he" for every applicant.
When speaking with residents who are more comfortable in Jamaican Creole (Patois), use plain words, listen with respect and let them speak as they prefer. Never mock or correct them.
Offer large print, readable fonts, audio and screen-reader versions on request.
Ask about access needs when booking interviews and meetings.

flow: Ask users with different needs what barriers they meet
Audit the building, forms, website, signs and staff practice with a checklist
List the barriers found and rank them by importance and cost
Agree an action plan with owners, dates and a budget
Make the changes and tell users about them
Review again with users, and keep improving

blocks.note: Ask the people who use the service. A checklist alone can miss barriers that users meet every day.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When a ministry designs a new programme, such as a youth employment scheme, consult youth groups, groups representing persons with disabilities, rural communities, women's groups and others who may be affected. Early consultation leads to better design and builds trust.

blocks.note: Jamaican Sign Language is the language of Deaf Jamaicans. Ask for a qualified interpreter, and where none is available, use written exchange or another agreed method. Check the agency's arrangements for interpreters in advance.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Seek **different views** and treat all staff fairly: show that you value diversity by what you do.
In meetings, invite each person's view in turn; use written ideas, small groups or pre-meeting notes so that quieter officers can contribute.
Rotate tasks such as minute-taking and representing the unit so that opportunities are shared.
Set an example in your own words and jokes.
Keep to the same standards of performance and conduct for everyone.

blocks.p: If staff make repeated jokes about a colleague's accent, or exclude a colleague because of a disability, **stop it, deal with it under policy and support the person affected**. Do not treat it as "just banter" and do not ask the person to "toughen up".

flow: Stop the behaviour at once and speak privately to those involved
Listen to the person affected and record the facts
Follow the agency's harassment and grievance procedure, with human resource advice
Protect the person who complained from any retaliation
Keep the matter confidential and review the outcome

blocks.p: If an officer complains that she was passed over for promotion because of her religion, **take it seriously and follow the grievance procedure**. Do not dismiss it or argue. People must be able to raise concerns in good faith without fear of bad treatment; this is why victimisation is unacceptable.
**Positive action** means lawful steps to encourage under-represented groups to apply or develop, without lowering standards or giving jobs to people who do not meet the requirements.

head: Positive action (acceptable)
Not acceptable
rows: Promoting a mentoring scheme that is open to all, but especially to women, who are under-represented in senior posts
Promoting an unqualified person because of their sex
Advertising posts in rural areas and through community groups
Setting a quota that overrides merit
Offering development to a group that has had fewer chances
Excluding a group from a scheme

ul: Practical cases, discussion and follow-up in teams change behaviour more than a one-off lecture.
An ongoing programme (short sessions, case discussion, manager coaching) reaches deeper than an event.
Support from senior managers is essential: they must take part and act on results.
**Aims**: what the body wants to achieve
**Scope**: who and what it covers (staff, applicants, service users, contractors)
**Responsibilities**: managers, HR, staff and the head of the agency
**How to raise concerns**: grievance and harassment procedures, and protection from retaliation
**How it will be monitored**: indicators, reports and review date

flow: Review the law and find where the agency has gaps
Consult staff, unions and service users
Draft the policy with HR and legal advice
Get approval from top management
Launch it, explain it in meetings and give training to all staff
Build it into recruitment, induction, appraisal and service standards
Monitor and review it each year

blocks.p: A policy launched two years ago that staff have never heard of has failed. The manager's first step is to **communicate it, train staff and build it into routines**.

ul: Collect data **voluntarily** and keep it **confidential**, so that staff trust it and the data protection law is met.
Use it only for its stated purpose and report it as totals, not as individuals.
Combine **numbers** (staff mix, applicants, hires, promotions) with **views** (staff survey, focus groups, grievances).
Compare trends over time, not a single figure.

head: Measure
Method
Worked example
rows: Share of a group
Number in group ÷ total × 100
42 women among 120 managers: 42 ÷ 120 = 0.35, so 35%
Share of applicants
Number from the group ÷ all applicants × 100
66 rural applicants among 300: 66 ÷ 300 = 0.22, so 22%
Selection rate
Hired from the group ÷ applied from the group × 100
40 applicants with a disability, 2 hired: 2 ÷ 40 = 5%; 360 other applicants, 36 hired: 36 ÷ 360 = 10%

blocks.p: A large gap in the selection rates, as in the last row, does not prove discrimination, but it is a signal that the process should be reviewed for barriers.

ul: If a staff survey shows that staff with disabilities feel less included, **discuss the results with staff and agree actions**.

If complaints of unfair treatment fall at the same time as survey responses fall, the fall in complaints may not mean less unfair treatment. People may have stopped reporting because they do not trust the process.
The best measures of progress are **trends in inclusion survey scores and the staff mix over time**.

blocks.p: A **diversity audit** is a planned review of a body's workforce, policies and services to find gaps in diversity and inclusion. Include recruitment records, promotion rates, pay, grievances, staff survey results, and accessibility of buildings, forms and communication.

ul: explain diversity, inclusion, equality and equity, with examples.
name visible and less visible differences and explain why diversity benefits a public body.
define stereotype, prejudice, unconscious bias, discrimination, harassment, victimisation and tokenism.
tell direct from indirect discrimination.
name the main laws and policies by purpose and say when to seek HR or legal advice.
keep confidential information, such as health conditions, private.
plan a fair recruitment process and avoid unlawful interview questions.
arrange reasonable accommodations after talking with the officer.
consider requests about family and religion fairly.
remove physical, communication and language barriers, and consult users.
use plain, inclusive language and respect Jamaican Creole and Jamaican Sign Language.
run meetings that hear every voice, and deal with unfair behaviour under policy.
explain positive action and tell it from quotas and tokenism.
write and launch a diversity and inclusion policy.
collect data voluntarily and confidentially, work out simple percentages and read the results with care.

terms: Diversity
The mix of differences among the people in a workforce and among those it serves.
Inclusion
Making sure every person feels valued, respected and able to take part fully.
Stereotype
A fixed, over-simple belief about what all members of a group are like.
Prejudice
An unfair opinion formed about a person or group before knowing the facts.
Unconscious bias
Attitudes and beliefs held without being aware of them.
Direct discrimination
Treating a person openly less well because of a personal characteristic.
Indirect discrimination
A rule that applies to all but puts one group at an unfair disadvantage and is not needed for the job.
Harassment
Unwanted conduct that violates a person's dignity or creates a hostile setting.
Victimisation
Treating a person badly because they raised or supported a complaint.
Reasonable accommodation
A change that allows a person with a disability to do the job or take part equally.
Accessibility
How easily people of all abilities can reach and use a building, service or document.
Positive action
Lawful steps to encourage under-represented groups to apply or develop, without lowering standards.
Tokenism
A small, surface effort made only to look inclusive.
Jamaican Sign Language (JSL)
The sign language used by Deaf people in Jamaica.
Diversity audit
A planned review of workforce, policies and services to find gaps in diversity and inclusion.

c1.title: Hiring clerks at a municipal corporation
c1.text: A municipal corporation in St Catherine is hiring six clerks. The advertisement appeared only in one daily newspaper, and the draft criteria include "must be under 30" and "own transport". Of 400 applicants, 60 came from rural parts of the parish; of these, 3 were shortlisted out of 40 shortlisted overall. The HR officer, Mrs Sonia Francis, asks the chair of the panel, Mr Anthony Reid, to prepare the interview. A panel member says that mothers of young children 'will not be reliable'.

c2.title: An officer with a disability in Mandeville
c2.text: A ministry's regional office in Mandeville has recruited Mr Delroy Gordon, an officer who uses a wheelchair, to a unit on the first floor of a building with no lift. The office manager, Mrs Beverley Chambers, notices that colleagues leave Mr Gordon out of the Friday lunch and sometimes joke about his 'slow chair'. Mr Gordon has not complained. In team meetings, three confident officers do most of the talking.

c3.title: A parish office that serves everyone
c3.text: The customer service centre of a municipal corporation in Falmouth serves many older residents, vendors and farmers. Some forms use long legal language. A Deaf resident, Ms Paulette Ellis, visits to query a bill and cannot be understood. An elderly farmer in the next queue prefers to speak Patois and says clerks 'talk down' to him. The manager, Mr Winston Dunn, plans to make the centre more accessible.

c4.title: A diversity policy at a statutory body
c4.text: A statutory body in Kingston with 300 staff launched a diversity policy two years ago, but most staff say they have never read it. A staff survey shows that staff with disabilities feel less included than others, and only 12 of the 75 senior posts are held by women, though women are 60% of all staff. The Human Resource Director, Mrs Hyacinth Lewis, plans a mentoring scheme for women, an inclusion survey and a confidential staff profile.

c5.title: Requests and a complaint in Montego Bay
c5.text: In a government agency in Montego Bay, Ms Camille Rowe, a Seventh-day Adventist officer, asks not to work from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset. Mr Trevor Wallace, a single father, asks to start an hour later to take his child to school. A third officer, Ms Alicia Brown, has told her manager that she was passed over for promotion because of her religion, and says a colleague has since been giving her the worst duties.

questions.q: Which change to the recruitment plan is most likely to attract rural applicants?
o: Advertise widely, including online and in rural communities
Advertise in the same daily newspaper for an extra week or two
Lower the entry standards that apply to rural applicants only
Hold all interviews at the main office in the evenings only
questions.why: Wider advertising reaches people who would not see a single newspaper advertisement, without lowering standards.

questions.q: The draft criteria say 'must be under 30'. What is the best action?
o: Keep it, because younger staff learn faster
Remove the age limit and use job-related criteria only
Change it to 'under 40' so that more people can apply
Keep it but accept older applicants with strong experience
questions.why: Age is not a genuine requirement for clerical work, so the criterion would discriminate. Use written, job-related criteria for all applicants.

questions.q: A panel member says mothers of young children 'will not be reliable'. What is this?
o: A sensible check of availability for the job
Direct discrimination against male applicants
A stereotype that leads to unfair bias
Indirect discrimination against older applicants
questions.why: It is a fixed belief about a whole group. Judge each applicant against the criteria; ask all candidates the same availability question if working hours matter.

questions.q: Of 400 applicants, 60 were rural, and 3 of the 40 shortlisted were rural. What do these figures suggest?
o: Rural applicants were shortlisted fairly because 3 is above zero
The process is sound because rural applicants were only 15% of applicants
The shortlist is unfair only if every rural applicant was left out of it
The process should be checked for barriers to rural applicants
questions.why: Rural applicants were 15% of applicants but 7.5% of the shortlist. This does not prove unfairness, but it signals a need to review the criteria and process.

questions.q: What should Mrs Chambers do first about Mr Gordon's upstairs unit?
o: Talk with him and arrange a ground-floor workspace
Tell him to use the stairs on the days when he can manage them
Ask him to work from home without first discussing it with him
Wait for him to make a formal complaint before changing anything
questions.why: People know what helps them, so ask first. The accommodation should not depend on the officer having to complain.

questions.q: Colleagues joke about his 'slow chair' and leave him out of lunches. What should Mrs Chambers do?
o: Ignore it because Mr Gordon has not complained
Stop it, deal with it under policy and support Mr Gordon
Tell Mr Gordon not to take the jokes so seriously
Hold a general talk on teamwork without naming the behaviour
questions.why: Repeated remarks and exclusion based on disability are unacceptable. A manager must act without waiting for a complaint, and she should support the person affected.

questions.q: Mrs Chambers often picks the same two outgoing officers to represent the office at workshops. What is the best way to share such opportunities?
o: Pick whoever is most senior in each case, as they know the work
Continue as before, since the two officers get good results
Rotate them fairly and tell all staff how people are chosen
Let staff volunteer, and choose the first officer who does so
questions.why: Opportunities spread fairly develop all staff and show that the office values everyone. A clear, open method also guards against favouritism and unconscious bias.

questions.q: Ms Ellis, a Deaf resident, cannot be understood at the counter. Which response best meets her needs?
o: Ask her to return the next day with a hearing relative to speak for her
Speak more slowly and loudly until she appears to understand the clerk
Hand her a copy of the bill and ask her to read it without discussion
Use a Jamaican Sign Language interpreter or exchange written notes
questions.why: A Deaf person communicates by sign or writing. Good practice is to arrange an interpreter, or write, and not to make her depend on others.

questions.q: A partially sighted resident asks for the notice on market fees. Which response is best?
o: Offer it in large print, or read it aloud or send an audio copy
Say that the notice is displayed on the board outside the office
Ask the resident to bring a relative who can read it later
Read out only the sections the clerk thinks are relevant to him
questions.why: Information must be offered in a form the person can use. Large print, audio or a screen-reader version removes the barrier, and the resident decides what he needs to hear.

questions.q: The elderly farmer prefers Patois and says clerks 'talk down' to him. Which approach is most respectful?
o: Ask him politely to speak in Standard English to avoid confusion
Use plain words, listen well and let him speak as he prefers
Use very simple, childlike words so that he can understand easily
Pass him to the youngest officer on duty, who may speak Patois
questions.why: Respecting how people speak builds trust. Plain words and attention, without patronising, show respect.

questions.q: Mr Dunn wants to make the centre more accessible. What should he do first?
o: Order new signs and a ramp straight away from the supplier he prefers
Ask the central office for a general report on access in all centres
Ask users with different needs what barriers they meet
Wait for formal complaints to show him what the main problems are
questions.why: Users know where the barriers are. Consulting them first ensures that money is spent on real problems.

questions.q: Who is responsible for making the diversity policy work in the statutory body?
o: Only the human resource unit, which owns all staff policies
Only the staff who have said that they have been treated unfairly
Only the Director, who signed and issued the policy two years ago
Everyone, with set duties for managers, HR and the agency head
questions.why: A policy works only when all staff follow it. Managers apply it day to day, HR advises and monitors, and top management is accountable for results.

questions.q: Of 75 senior posts, 12 are held by women, though women are 60% of the 300 staff. What percentage of senior posts do women hold?
questions.why: 12 ÷ 75 = 0.16, or 16%. Women are 60% of staff but 16% of senior posts, a gap that should be investigated.

questions.q: Mrs Lewis plans a diversity audit. Which set of records should it include?
o: Only the number of staff in each grade at the date of the audit
Recruitment, promotion, grievance and survey records, and access
Only the complaints that were upheld by the grievance panel
Only the pay scale for each grade and the budget for training
questions.why: An audit looks at the whole picture: who is recruited and promoted, what staff say, what complaints show and whether buildings, forms and communication are accessible.

questions.q: The statutory body will collect a confidential staff profile. How should this be done?
o: Compulsorily, with each name recorded so that results can be checked later
Voluntarily, with the names of staff passed on to every line manager
Voluntarily, reported as totals, and used only for its stated purpose
Compulsorily, with the results kept on an open shared drive for HR staff
questions.why: Staff will only share if they trust that the data is private. Data protection law requires careful, limited use and secure storage.

questions.q: Ms Rowe asks not to work from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset. What should her manager do?
o: Refuse, since the roster must be the same for every officer in the unit
Approve it at once without checking the needs of the service
Tell her to take annual leave on those days instead of working them
Consider it fairly and adjust the roster if the work allows
questions.why: Religious observance is a protected matter. The manager should look for a workable roster fairly without harming the service.

questions.q: The agency approves Mr Wallace's later start for three months. Another officer asks for the same arrangement for her own child. What should the manager do?
o: Consider hers as fairly as his, against the needs of the work
Refuse, since the first arrangement was a special favour
Approve it automatically so that the two officers are equal
Refuse until Mr Wallace's arrangement has ended in three months
questions.why: Fair treatment means the same careful consideration for everyone, weighing the work needs each time. It does not mean automatic approval or automatic refusal.

questions.q: The grievance on promotion is being investigated. Which evidence is most useful in judging whether religion affected the decision?
o: The opinions of colleagues about both candidates' religion
The written criteria, each candidate's scores and the panel's notes
Ms Brown's attendance record for the past year only
The length of service of each candidate on the shortlist
questions.why: A fair decision should be traceable to criteria and scores. Written records show whether the same standards were applied to everyone.

questions.q: Ms Brown says a colleague has since given her the worst duties. What is this likely to be?
o: The normal rotation of duties in a busy unit with limited staff
Direct discrimination against the colleague who allocated the duties
Victimisation, which must be stopped and investigated
Positive action to help Ms Brown develop in her career in the agency
questions.why: Treating someone badly after they raise a complaint is victimisation. Staff must be protected so that they are not afraid to report problems.

questions.q: An agency requires every applicant for an office-based post to hold a driver's licence, though the job involves no driving. Several qualified applicants with disabilities cannot meet it. What is this?
o: Direct discrimination, because the agency named disability as the reason
Positive action, since the agency has set a clear standard for all
A lawful condition, because the rule is applied equally to everyone
Possible indirect discrimination, as the job does not need it
questions.why: A rule applied to all that puts one group at a disadvantage and is not needed for the job may be indirect discrimination. The test is the effect and the job need, not whether the rule looks equal.
